title: Engines and humans 5: top players, centaurs and your own habits
outcomes: Explains how preparation, advanced chess, freestyle and correspondence chess use engines, naming the source for each fact
Reads a Berlin endgame structure and says why the position limits attacks
Chooses between equal engine moves by asking what plan each starts, and says what to do when the opponent leaves the prepared line
Shows a fortress where material misleads, using a tablebase result
Writes a plan for their own engine habits with five specific choices

steps.prompt: Before the numbers: in our database of top-level games (329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more), take the position after Black's third move, the knight to f6, in this Ruy Lopez. What share of the games that reached it went all the way to the queenless position at the end of the line? Guess, and say how sure you are.

steps.text: **What the data says [V].** Of 4,911 games in which White castled on move four, 4,874 saw Black take the e-pawn. Then 2,263 pushed the d-pawn, 2,240 reached the knight retreat, 1,270 took on c6, and 1,243 reached the queenless position: about one in four of the castling games. Several later moves are forced recaptures, so repeating a line does not prove preparation [I]; that strong players chose it so often suggests it [H]. What is left for a human to decide?

steps.text: **The wall.** With the queens off, nobody has a direct mating attack on Black's king, and White's four-against-three kingside majority needs many moves to create a passed pawn [I]. Black's bishop pair is a lasting asset [I], and the engine rates the position as level [V]. The setup is nicknamed the Berlin Wall [R]. Wikipedia's page on the Berlin Defence says Kramnik played it in four games of his 2000 match with Kasparov, all drawn [R: recalled, not rechecked here].

steps.text: **Preparation is memory plus a reason.** Players keep files of engine-checked lines, and a *novelty* is the first move that leaves the files [R]. Engines check lines deeper than a person can calculate, so the first twenty moves can be learned like a poem. [I] The danger is the first move after the poem ends. If you only remember moves, you have nothing to ask; if you know what each side wants, you can still make a plan.

steps.caption: The other main road at this point: the rook move. In our data it was played 2,553 times against 2,263 for the pawn push [V]. Another way to reach a level game: White attacks the knight at once and, after Black's knight retreat, regains the e-pawn. The move order differs from the main line.

steps.text: **What each move is for [I].** h3 takes g4 from Black's bishop, so d4 can follow without a pin; the risk is a slow start. a4 hits b5; the risk is that b4 then gains Black space. d4 fights for the centre at once; the risk is opening lines before the pieces are ready. d3 keeps things solid; the risk is passivity. Black's usual plans: knight to a5 to challenge the bishop, c5 for space, a bishop move such as g4 or b7, rook to e8.

steps.text: **Advanced chess.** Kasparov and Topalov played a 3-3 advanced-chess match, each with a computer beside them, in León in 1998 [S: Wikipedia]. Kasparov later argued, in a 2010 essay, that a person plus a machine plus a good process can beat either alone [R, not checked against the full text]. People who combine human and machine this way are called *centaurs* [R].

steps.caption: A tactic from Morphy's Opera Game (Paris, 1858) [R]. A machine finds mates like this at once [I], so in centaur play the human's time goes to plans. The mate in two, on a board.

line.say: The queen gives check and offers itself; the knight is the only piece that can take it.
The knight takes the queen, and in doing so leaves the d-file.
The rook mates: the bishop on g5 guards d8, and the king has no flight square.

claims.statement: The queen move to b8 leads to a forced mate in two.

steps.text: **Freestyle.** In this lesson freestyle means human-plus-engine teams, not the shuffled-start Chess960 format also sold under that name [S]. Wikipedia dates the idea to a 2004 blitz event [S, to confirm]. Kasparov's 2010 essay, known to me only from a summary [R], describes a 2005 online tournament won by two amateurs with several computers, ahead of grandmaster teams. His reading: a better *process* won. [H] One tournament shows what is possible, not what usually happens.

steps.prompt: Classify each practice: preparation, centaur or advanced chess, correspondence chess, or cheating. Choose one label for each.

steps.text: **Check yourself.** Studying a file is preparation. Playing with a program under the rules is centaur or advanced chess. Correspondence chess is run by a federation: the ICCF allows engines and tablebases, even in its World Championship, and Wikipedia says draw rates are very high [S]. An engine in a game that bans it is cheating. The event's rules decide.

steps.caption: Correspondence thinking [H]: the main line is level, but there is a quieter option that keeps more pieces on. Step through the d3 line; the engine rates it about as well.

steps.text: **Where numbers mislead.** An engine score is one number. [I] Without a tablebase, it can look winning on a fortress that cannot be won; here the tablebase solves each position for us, and the lesson is that counting material is not a verdict. [H] People may still add the most in long plans where the score hardly changes; our boards are tablebase positions, not human wins. Predict the three positions below.

steps.title: Does the wrong-coloured bishop save the lone king?
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position is a bishop and h-pawn against a bare king, the bishop on a light square. In the second the bishop stands on a dark square, the colour of h8. In the third the white king stands one rank further back, on f5. Which change matters?

steps.text: **The usual plan split [R].** In closed King's Indian positions like this, White typically plays on the queenside with pawn pushes such as b4 and c5, while Black plays on the kingside with f5 and later g5. This is widely taught; I have not checked it against a named book here. [I] That is why Rb1 and a3 serve one wing, while Be3 and Ne1 prepare for Black's f-pawn push.

steps.text: **Human-like play.** Maia networks are trained on Lichess games to play the move a human of a given rating would choose, not the best move [V: our research notes]; our Play page offers one as an optional opponent [V: project docs]. [H] A model of human error could help in two ways: training against the mistakes you will really meet, and fair-play checks that ask whether a move looks like what a player of that rating would do. No evidence here that it works; it is a hypothesis.

**What coaches say [S, not checked against the books].** Per Wikipedia and a chess.com article, Jeremy Silman puts a tactical check first and holds that engine analysis shows what to play but not why. Per a chess.com blog review of Aagaard's *Excelling at Chess Calculation* (2004), he argues that the worst errors often come when a key candidate move is overlooked. [I] Both fit *engine-last*. Neither is a top player describing his own engine use; that part is [H] here.

steps.text: **Risks.** [I] If the engine always names the move, you stop practising the search for candidates. [H] A second risk is trusting a number: a score does not say which plan your opponent will find hard. The third is fair play: using an engine where it is banned breaks the rules and the point of playing. Rules differ by event, since some allow engines, so check before you use one.

**Your engine habits.** A habit is a rule you decide in advance. Fill in the form: when you check, what you write first, what you look for, how often, and what you never do. Make each answer short enough to follow when you are tired. [H] A plan you will keep beats a perfect plan you will not.

steps.text: **Answers.** The first is supported (Wikipedia). The second is contradicted: according to the sources in lesson 1, Deep Blue won in 1997. The third is contradicted: Wikipedia places the start of freestyle in a 2004 blitz event by Ingo Althoefer and Timo Klaustermeyer. The fourth is supported by Wikipedia as I recall it [R]. The fifth is not supported: we have no source, and our own note calls the idea a hypothesis.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say when an engine helps and when it hurts? Did you give an example a beginner could set up on a board, such as the bishop and h-pawn against a bare king? Did you name one risk and one rule of your own? Did you mark what you know and what you only suspect? A sample strong answer: 'Write your own view first, then check [I]; an engine finds tactics well but cannot say what you understand.' The app does not grade this.

**Recap.**
- Engines changed preparation: lines are memorised deep, so know *why* each side plays them.
- Level scores hide different plans; you choose.
- Centaur and correspondence chess show process can matter.
- Some positions, like fortresses, fool the count.
- Think first, engine last (this series: lesson 1 on history, lesson 2 on what engines see and miss, and this one).
- [H] People may still add most in long plans.
- Write your habits down.
